blocks.prompt: 2 (i) Find the domain of the following: \(f(x) = \sin^{-1}(5x - 3)\).
blocks.explanation:
\(\sin^{-1}\) accepts only inputs from \(-1\) to \(1\).
So the whole input \(5x - 3\) must lie in \([-1, 1]\). Solve this double inequality for \(x\), as in Example 3.
steps:
Given: \(f(x) = \sin^{-1}(5x - 3)\).
To find: the domain of \(f\).
Method: The domain of \(\sin^{-1} u\) is \(-1 \le u \le 1\). Put \(u = 5x - 3\) and solve the double inequality.

Write the condition
\[-1 \le 5x - 3 \le 1\]
Why: \(\sin^{-1}\) is defined only for inputs in \([-1, 1]\).

Solve for x
\[2 \le 5x \le 4\]
\[\frac{2}{5} \le x \le \frac{4}{5}\]
Why: Add 3 to all three parts, then divide all parts by 5 (positive, so the signs stay).

Check
\[x = \tfrac{2}{5}: \; 5x - 3 = -1\]
\[x = \tfrac{4}{5}: \; 5x - 3 = 1\]
Why: The end points give exactly \(-1\) and \(1\), the ends of the allowed input.

blocks.prompt: 2 (ii) Find the domain of the following: \(g(x) = \cos^{-1}\sqrt{x - 3}\).
blocks.explanation:
Two conditions: the square root needs \(x - 3 \ge 0\), and \(\cos^{-1}\) needs its input in \([-1, 1]\).
Since a square root is never negative, the second condition becomes \(0 \le \sqrt{x - 3} \le 1\).
steps:
Given: \(g(x) = \cos^{-1}\sqrt{x - 3}\).
To find: the domain of \(g\).
Method: Need \(\sqrt{x - 3}\) to be real and to lie in \([-1, 1]\). Square the inequality (all parts are non-negative).

Condition for the square root
\[x - 3 \ge 0 \Rightarrow x \ge 3\]
Why: The square root of a negative number is not real.

Condition for the inverse cosine
\[-1 \le \sqrt{x - 3} \le 1\]
\[0 \le \sqrt{x - 3} \le 1\]
Why: \(\cos^{-1}\) needs its input in \([-1, 1]\), and \(\sqrt{x - 3} \ge 0\) always, so the left end is really 0.

Square and solve
\[0 \le x - 3 \le 1\]
\[3 \le x \le 4\]
Why: All parts are non-negative, so squaring keeps the order. Then add 3.

Check
\[x = 4: \; \sqrt{1} = 1, \; \cos^{-1}1 = 0\]
\[x = 5: \; \sqrt{2} > 1 \text{ (not allowed)}\]
Why: The end point works and a value just outside fails.

blocks.prompt: 2 (iii) Find the domain of the following: \(h(x) = \csc^{-1}(x^2 - 3)\).
blocks.explanation:
\(\csc^{-1}\) accepts inputs \(\le -1\) or \(\ge 1\) (domain \((-\infty, -1] \cup [1, \infty)\)).
So \(x^2 - 3 \ge 1\) or \(x^2 - 3 \le -1\). Solve both cases and take their union, because either case is enough.
steps:
Given: \(h(x) = \csc^{-1}(x^2 - 3)\).
To find: the domain of \(h\).
Method: The domain of \(\csc^{-1} u\) is \(u \le -1\) or \(u \ge 1\). Put \(u = x^2 - 3\), solve each case, and join the answers (union).

Write the condition
\[x^2 - 3 \ge 1 \quad \text{or} \quad x^2 - 3 \le -1\]
Why: \(\csc^{-1}\) is not defined for inputs strictly between \(-1\) and \(1\).

Case A
\[x^2 - 3 \ge 1 \Rightarrow x^2 \ge 4\]
\[(x - 2)(x + 2) \ge 0\]
\[x \le -2 \text{ or } x \ge 2\]
Why: A product is \(\ge 0\) when both factors have the same sign: both negative (\(x \le -2\)) or both positive (\(x \ge 2\)).

Case B
\[x^2 - 3 \le -1 \Rightarrow x^2 \le 2\]
\[(x - \sqrt{2})(x + \sqrt{2}) \le 0\]
\[-\sqrt{2} \le x \le \sqrt{2}\]
Why: A product is \(\le 0\) when the factors have opposite signs, which happens between the roots.

Join the two cases
\[(-\infty, -2] \cup [-\sqrt{2}, \sqrt{2}] \cup [2, \infty)\]
Why: The condition says 'or', so every \(x\) from either case belongs to the domain.

Check
\[x = 2: \; \csc^{-1}(1) = \tfrac{\pi}{2}\]
\[x = 0: \; \csc^{-1}(-3) \text{ exists}\]
\[x = 1.7: \; x^2 - 3 = -0.11 \text{ (not allowed)}\]
Why: Values from both cases work; a value with \(\sqrt{2} < |x| < 2\) puts the input inside \((-1, 1)\). The figure shows the same picture.

answer_figure.alt: Parabola y = x squared minus 3 with the band between y = minus 1 and y = 1 shaded. The curve is allowed where it is outside the band: for x at most minus 2, between minus root 2 and root 2, and for x at least 2. These three pieces are marked in green on the x-axis.
answer_figure.caption: Domain of h: the parabola y = x² − 3 must stay outside the band −1 < y < 1 (original drawing).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The answer key (Answers 9.1) prints \(-\sqrt{2} \le x \le \sqrt{2}\). This is incomplete: it is only Case B (\(x^2 - 3 \le -1\)). Case A (\(x^2 - 3 \ge 1\), i.e. \(|x| \ge 2\)) is left out, although for example \(h(2) = \csc^{-1}(1) = \frac{\pi}{2}\) is defined. The correct domain is \((-\infty, -2] \cup [-\sqrt{2}, \sqrt{2}] \cup [2, \infty)\).

blocks.prompt: 2 (iv) Find the domain of the following: \(k(x) = \sin^{-1}(\ln x)\).
blocks.explanation:
Two conditions: \(\ln x\) needs \(x > 0\), and \(\sin^{-1}\) needs \(-1 \le \ln x \le 1\).
Undo the logarithm with the exponential function, as in Example 3(iii).
steps:
Given: \(k(x) = \sin^{-1}(\ln x)\).
To find: the domain of \(k\).
Method: Need \(x > 0\) and \(-1 \le \ln x \le 1\). Apply \(e^{(\,)}\) to all parts.

Write the condition
\[-1 \le \ln x \le 1\]
Why: The input of \(\sin^{-1}\) must lie in \([-1, 1]\).

Remove the logarithm
\[e^{-1} \le e^{\ln x} \le e^{1}\]
\[\frac{1}{e} \le x \le e\]
Why: \(e^{t}\) is an increasing function, so applying it keeps the inequality signs; \(e^{\ln x} = x\).

The log condition
\[\frac{1}{e} > 0\]
Why: All these \(x\) are positive, so \(\ln x\) is defined; the condition \(x > 0\) adds nothing new.

Check
\[x = e: \; \sin^{-1}(\ln e) = \sin^{-1}1 = \tfrac{\pi}{2}\]
Why: The end point gives an allowed input.

blocks.prompt: 2 (v) Find the domain of the following: \(p(x) = \tan^{-1}\sqrt{4 - x^2}\).
blocks.explanation:
\(\tan^{-1}\) accepts every real number, so it puts no restriction.
The only condition comes from the square root: \(4 - x^2 \ge 0\).
steps:
Given: \(p(x) = \tan^{-1}\sqrt{4 - x^2}\).
To find: the domain of \(p\).
Method: The domain of \(\tan^{-1}\) is \((-\infty, \infty)\), so only the square root matters.

Condition for the square root
\[4 - x^2 \ge 0 \Rightarrow x^2 \le 4\]
Why: The square root of a negative number is not real.

Solve
\[(x - 2)(x + 2) \le 0\]
\[-2 \le x \le 2\]
Why: The product is negative or zero between the roots \(-2\) and \(2\).

Check
\[x = 2: \; \tan^{-1}\sqrt{0} = 0\]
\[x = 3: \; \sqrt{-5} \text{ is not real}\]
Why: The end point works and a value outside fails.

blocks.prompt: 2 (vi) Find the domain of the following: \(q(x) = \sec^{-1}(x + 2)\).
blocks.explanation:
\(\sec^{-1}\) accepts inputs \(\le -1\) or \(\ge 1\).
So \(x + 2 \le -1\) or \(x + 2 \ge 1\); solve both and take the union.
steps:
Given: \(q(x) = \sec^{-1}(x + 2)\).
To find: the domain of \(q\).
Method: The domain of \(\sec^{-1} u\) is \((-\infty, -1] \cup [1, \infty)\). Put \(u = x + 2\).

Case A
\[x + 2 \le -1 \Rightarrow x \le -3\]
Why: Subtract 2 from both sides.

Case B
\[x + 2 \ge 1 \Rightarrow x \ge -1\]
Why: Subtract 2 from both sides.

Join the cases
\[(-\infty, -3] \cup [-1, \infty)\]
Why: Either case is enough ('or').

Check
\[x = -2: \; x + 2 = 0 \text{ (not allowed)}\]
Why: Values between \(-3\) and \(-1\) give inputs inside \((-1, 1)\), so they are excluded.

blocks.prompt: 2 (vii) Find the domain of the following: \(u(x) = \sec^{-1}\left(\frac{3x - 1}{2}\right)\).
blocks.explanation:
Again the input of \(\sec^{-1}\) must be \(\le -1\) or \(\ge 1\).
Solve \(\frac{3x - 1}{2} \le -1\) and \(\frac{3x - 1}{2} \ge 1\) separately and take the union.
steps:
Given: \(u(x) = \sec^{-1}\left(\frac{3x - 1}{2}\right)\).
To find: the domain of \(u\).
Method: Domain of \(\sec^{-1}\) is \((-\infty, -1] \cup [1, \infty)\). Solve each case by multiplying by 2 (positive).

Case A
\[\frac{3x - 1}{2} \le -1\]
\[3x - 1 \le -2 \Rightarrow 3x \le -1\]
\[x \le -\frac{1}{3}\]
Why: Multiply by 2, add 1, divide by 3; all positive steps, so the sign stays.

Case B
\[\frac{3x - 1}{2} \ge 1\]
\[3x - 1 \ge 2 \Rightarrow 3x \ge 3\]
\[x \ge 1\]
Why: Same steps.

Join the cases
\[\left(-\infty, -\frac{1}{3}\right] \cup [1, \infty)\]
Why: Either case is enough ('or').

Check
\[x = 1: \; \tfrac{3 - 1}{2} = 1, \; \sec^{-1}1 = 0\]
\[x = 0: \; -\tfrac{1}{2} \text{ (not allowed)}\]
Why: The end point works; a value between the two pieces does not.

blocks.prompt: 2 (viii) Find the domain of the following: \(v(x) = \sin^{-1}(\ln x) + \csc^{-1}(e^{x})\).
blocks.explanation:
A sum is defined only where both terms are defined.
Find the domain of each term separately, then take their intersection (common part).
steps:
Given: \(v(x) = \sin^{-1}(\ln x) + \csc^{-1}(e^{x})\).
To find: the domain of \(v\).
Method: Domain of a sum = intersection of the domains of the two terms.

First term
\[-1 \le \ln x \le 1 \Rightarrow \frac{1}{e} \le x \le e\]
Why: Same as part (iv): apply the increasing function \(e^{t}\) to all parts.

Second term
\[e^{x} \le -1 \quad \text{or} \quad e^{x} \ge 1\]
\[e^{x} \ge 1 = e^{0} \Rightarrow x \ge 0\]
Why: The domain of \(\csc^{-1}\) is \((-\infty, -1] \cup [1, \infty)\). \(e^{x} > 0\) for every \(x\), so \(e^{x} \le -1\) is impossible.

Intersection
\[\left[\frac{1}{e}, e\right] \cap [0, \infty)\]
\[= \left[\frac{1}{e}, e\right]\]
Why: \(\frac{1}{e} \approx 0.37 > 0\), so the whole first interval already lies in \([0, \infty)\).

Check
\[x = \tfrac{1}{e}: \; \ln x = -1, \; e^{x} \approx 1.44 \ge 1\]
Why: At the left end both terms are defined, so \(\frac{1}{e}\) belongs to the domain. The answer key's \(\left[\frac{1}{e}, e\right]\) is correct.

answer_figure.alt: Three number lines. The first marks the closed interval from 1 over e (about 0.37) to e (about 2.72) needed by inverse sine of ln x. The second marks x greater than or equal to 0 needed by inverse cosecant of e to the x. The third shows their common part, the interval from 1 over e to e.
answer_figure.caption: Domain of v: the common part (intersection) of the two separate domains (original drawing).
